scenarios.title: The Requirement That Wasn't
scenarios.anchor: Challenges assumptions, reframes and holds a point of view
scenarios.blurb: Sign-off is on Friday. The spec says 'notify the customer', everyone has signed, and nobody has asked what happens when the customer has no phone number. Four decisions, about ten minutes.

intro.title: What is this scenario about?
intro.text: This one trains anchor 7 of Swanubhava™ - challenging assumptions and holding a point of view. In plain words: when everyone in the room agrees, someone still has to ask 'are we all agreeing on the same thing?' Obviously that is easy to say in a classroom. It is much harder two days before a sign-off, when one question feels like slowing everyone down. You will play the product analyst. There are four decisions and one short piece of writing. There are no trick answers here - but some answers are expensive. A small honest note: the company and the numbers are made up. The pattern is not - I have seen it more times than I would like to admit.

brief.title: Two days to sign-off
brief.text: You are the product analyst (PA) on a refunds release for an online retailer. Today, customers find out about an approved refund only when the money shows up in their account - so support gets about 400 'where is my refund?' calls every week. This release is meant to fix that. The line that matters in the spec reads: 'When a refund is approved, notify the customer.' Meera from operations has signed it. Arjun, the tech lead, has estimated it at three days. Priya, the sponsor, has already told the support head that the calls will drop this quarter. Everyone is comfortable. You are not - and you cannot yet say why.

room.title: Everyone nods
room.text: In the stand-up, Priya says: 'We are in good shape. Let's not reopen anything that is already agreed.' Everyone nods. Arjun is already breaking the work into tasks. You read the line once more - 'notify the customer'. Notify how? By SMS? Email? Both? You are not sure whether this is a real problem or you are just being fussy. (Every PA asks themselves that question at least once a week. I certainly did.)

n1.prompt: Sign-off is Friday. What do you do with that discomfort?

choices.label: Let it go - it is one line, and everyone has signed

consequence.title: Week three of production
consequence.text: The release goes out on time. Refunds are approved, messages go out, and the calls start to drop. Then a customer with no mobile number on file gets nothing at all. She calls support twice, then writes to the consumer forum. The ticket lands back on your desk with a severity tag - and a question from Priya: 'Did nobody think of this?'
consequence.lesson: Everyone signing the same line does not mean everyone read it the same way. Agreement can hide confusion; it does not remove it. Your discomfort was a cue - the kind an experienced person learns to trust - and you let it go because the date felt more important.

choices.label: Ask Meera for one real refund from last week, and exactly what that customer received

consequence.title: The example does the work
consequence.text: Meera pulls up a refund from last Tuesday. 'Notify' meant an SMS. Then she checks the numbers: about one in nine customers has no mobile number on file. Nobody had decided what those customers get. Meera had assumed SMS, Arjun had assumed email, and Priya had assumed 'something automatic'. It was never a disagreement. It was a blank.
consequence.lesson: A real example does what a review meeting cannot. Ask 'is this clear?' and everyone says yes. Ask 'what happened last Tuesday?' and the gaps show up on their own. Also notice what you did not do - you did not tell anyone their requirement was bad. You asked for a fact.

choices.label: Send the spec around again and ask everyone to re-read it carefully

consequence.title: Three replies, all 'looks fine'
consequence.text: Within the hour you get three thumbs-up emojis. Nobody read it again - why would they? They had already agreed. The line still means SMS to Meera, email to Arjun and 'something automatic' to Priya. And the round trip cost you half a day.
consequence.lesson: Re-reading the same words gives the same understanding. If you want a different answer, ask a different question - not the same question to more people.

n2.prompt: Thursday morning. You have twenty minutes with Meera and Arjun. Which of these must be settled before Friday? Pick every one that matters.

options.label: Which channel counts as a notification
options.sub: SMS, email, in-app, or any of them

options.label: What happens when the chosen channel is unavailable for that customer
The wording of the notification message
Who owns the decision when the channel fails
Which font the message template uses

n2.successNote: Right. The channel, what happens when that channel fails, and who decides. These three change what Arjun builds. The wording of the message and the font can be sorted later - they do not change the build.
n2.missNote: Before Friday you still need to settle:

criteria.label: Names the actual channel instead of 'notify'
criteria.hint: say which channel actually sends the message
criteria.coach: name the channel that actually fires - 'notify' is the word that let three people imagine three different things, and replacing it with 'SMS' or 'email' is what closes the gap

criteria.label: Says what happens when that channel is not available
criteria.hint: the customer with no number on file
criteria.coach: say what happens to the customer with no mobile number on file - that is the one in nine who would get silence in production, and a requirement that ignores them is where the complaint comes from

criteria.label: Says who or what decides when it fails
criteria.hint: who owns the call when it fails
criteria.coach: name who or what makes the call when the channel fails - if nobody owns an edge case, whoever is on shift at 6pm decides it quietly, and you will never know

n3.passNote: Channel, the failure case and the owner. Nobody can build that line two ways.
n3.speaker: Arjun, the tech lead
n3.question: Fine. Write me the line. If two developers read it, I want them to build the same thing.
n3.title: Write the line
n3.model: When a refund is approved, the system sends the customer an SMS to the mobile number on file. If no mobile number is on file, it sends the same notification by email instead. If neither is available, the refund is flagged to the ops queue and ops owns the decision on how the customer is told.
n3.modelExplain: This covers all three: it names the channel (SMS), handles the customer with no number (email fallback), and names the owner when both fail (ops). Edit it, or submit it as it is to see the grade.

n4.prompt: Thursday, 5pm. Priya reads your new line and frowns: 'An email fallback and an ops queue? That is scope creep. Sign the original line tomorrow, and we will do the rest in phase 2.' What do you do?

choices.label: Agree - it is her call, and phase 2 is only a month away

consequence.title: Phase 2, six weeks later
consequence.text: Phase 2 slips, the way phase 2 usually does. For six weeks, one in nine customers gets no message at all. The 'where is my refund?' calls you were meant to remove keep coming - from exactly the customers who are hardest to reach. Priya asks why the numbers have not moved.
consequence.lesson: Respecting the sponsor's decision is right. But she decided without knowing the cost, and you did know it. Holding a point of view is not about winning the argument. It is about making sure the person who decides can see what you can see.

choices.label: Put the cost in one line - 'one in nine customers will get nothing' - and ask her to decide with that in front of her
choices.sub: Make the cost visible, let her decide

consequence.title: One number changes the room
consequence.text: Priya goes quiet for a moment. 'One in nine? Those are the calls I promised to cut.' She asks Arjun how long the email fallback will take. 'Half a day.' She signs the full line on Friday.
consequence.lesson: You did not argue and you did not escalate. You put one fact in front of the person who owns the decision, and let her make it - this time with the facts. That is what holding a point of view looks like in real life: firm on the facts, open on the decision.

choices.label: Escalate to her manager - the risk is too big to leave with her

consequence.title: Right risk, wrong route
consequence.text: Her manager agrees with you and asks Priya why she did not know. The fallback gets built. The next sprint, Priya stops inviting you to her planning meetings.
consequence.lesson: You were right about the risk and wrong about the route. Escalation is for when the owner has seen the facts and still chooses something unsafe. Priya had not seen them yet - nobody had shown her.

good.title: The blank had nowhere to hide
good.moral: A good requirement is not one everyone agrees with. It is one nobody can misread.
good.verdict: You shipped on Friday, and the one-in-nine customer got a clear outcome instead of silence. Your line became the test case, which is why QA found nothing in week three. Now the question I would ask you in the debrief: where in your own work is a line that everyone has signed, and nobody has tested with a real example?
revealed: The probe
You asked for a real refund instead of asking whether the spec was clear.
The gap
You separated what had to be settled before Friday from what could wait.
The write-up
Channel, failure case and owner - all three in one line.
The line you held
You showed the sponsor the cost and let her decide with it in front of her.
Take this with you
When everyone agrees too quickly, ask for one real example.

deferred.title: Right line, wrong week
deferred.moral: Knowing the cost and keeping it to yourself is still a decision.
deferred.verdict: You did the hard part - you found the gap and wrote a line nobody could misread. Then you let it go at the last step. In the debrief, think about this: what would you have needed to feel comfortable putting that one number in front of Priya?
revealed: What held
You found the gap and wrote it down properly.
What slipped
You let the decision be made without the cost on the table.
Take this with you
Firm on the facts, open on the decision.

bruised.title: Shipped, with a bruise
bruised.moral: Being right is half the job. How you are right is the other half.
bruised.verdict: The customers are covered and the line is solid. But you spent trust you will need next quarter. In the debrief, ask yourself: what would one conversation with Priya, with the number in hand, have changed?
revealed: What held
You found the gap and wrote a line nobody could misread.
What slipped
You escalated before the owner had seen the facts.
Take this with you
Show the owner first. Escalate only if they still choose something unsafe.

partial.title: Better, but still readable two ways
partial.moral: Confusion does not announce itself. It shows up as a support ticket in week three.
partial.verdict: Your line is sharper than the original, but a developer reading it still has a decision left to make - and they will make it quietly, at 6pm, without you. Try the scenario again and see what changes when the line names the channel, the failure case and the owner.
revealed: What held
You found the gap before sign-off, which is most of the job.
What slipped
The written line still left at least one thing to interpretation.
